commentary.bottom_line: Two studies test parts of this practice, and neither measures whether review, correction, deletion, or opt-out controls reduce privacy harm in a deployed clinical AI system. One simulated study links greater data autonomy to more self-disclosure, and one benchmark suggests patient-level data deletion from deployed models may be technically feasible at small accuracy cost.

perspectives.view: The two tests are a level 4 simulated VR study (n=90, plus a survey of 152 patients) and a level 5 automated benchmark, and both provide indirect evidence. One measures self-disclosure and trust rather than privacy harm, and the other measures deletion speed and accuracy. Neither evaluates the full set of controls in real use, so certainty is very low.

The hazard studies show that the failure mode exists. Only 2 of 12 chatbot apps let users disable data sharing at sign-up. LLM outputs disclosed sensitive information in 722 of 2,113 documents (34.2%) despite do-not-share requests. These findings suggest that preference settings alone may not stop disclosure unless the model reliably honors them.

On 1,646,139 EHR records, sharded retraining (SISA) removed individual patient data 8.9 times faster than full retraining (7.5 s vs 66.7 s), with a 0.024% accuracy cost. On a genomic dataset it was 9.8 times faster, with a 0.048% cost. This suggests deletion requests may be workable for some model types, although the benchmark did not test live clinical workflows.

The benchmark reports deletion times measured in seconds for antimicrobial resistance models. This may indicate that honoring deletion requests need not require costly full retraining for similar models. The study did not examine staffing, request-handling procedures, or costs for larger generative models.

In the German study, mental health participants given more control over their data disclosed more to an AI therapist, but their trust did not change. This result suggests patients may share more when they hold control. The chatbot app review found that most apps offered users little control over their personal data.

The two tests were conducted in a German laboratory sample and on a benchmark dataset without reported demographics. Neither reports inclusion of Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. It is therefore unknown whether these groups can find and use data-control interfaces.

commentary.research_gap: No study has evaluated review, correction, deletion, opt-out, and preference controls together in a deployed clinical AI system with privacy-harm outcomes. It is also unknown whether models enforce stated preferences in their outputs, given 34.2% disclosure despite requests, and whether deletion methods work for large generative models.
commentary.underserved_note: Neither test included or reported Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy participants, so the evidence cannot show whether data-control interfaces are usable or effective for these populations. Controls that depend on reading privacy dashboards or English-language consent text may be less accessible to them, and no study has tested this.
